summary:
Short, source-only turn that settles a vocabulary question repeatedly relevant to earlier work: what the node's three progress accessors actually mean and which value bounds snapshot metadata (valid:true).

Finding recorded as a behaviour plus an explained investigation, with no defect claim:
`LastIndex` is stable storage — `getLastIndex` returns the maximum of the stored log index and the snapshot index under the last-index lock (state.go:159-163); `CommitIndex` is the committed index; and `AppliedIndex` is a dispatch watermark, not an FSM-completion one — its documentation (api.go:1238-1244) says it reflects the last index sent to the FSM over the apply channel and that the application's state may lag behind it, which matches the write site: `processLogs` advances the applied index after queueing the batch to the FSM thread (raft.go:1352-1358). A client that waits on its own `Apply` or `Barrier` future is answered by the FSM thread instead, so the caveat is about polling. Snapshot metadata does not use any of these accessors: the FSM thread reports the index it has accounted for with the snapshot request (fsm.go:216-233) and `takeSnapshot` refuses to snapshot when that index is below the committed configuration index (snapshot.go:125-211) — a fourth value that bounds what a snapshot may claim.

The counterevidence considered and rejected as a defect: the natural candidate (an accessor whose name promises more than the value delivers) is explicitly disclaimed in the accessor's own documentation, and the snapshot path was already verified separately to use the FSM thread's index with an explicit guard. Limitations are stated: source-only synthesis, no concurrent measurement of the four values, and no measurement of how far the applied watermark can lead a slow FSM. Nothing earlier is superseded — the entry exists so future reasoning does not treat these values as interchangeable.
